newsitem.title: GERMANY: German tax reform should cover capital gains - CDU.
newsitem.headline: German tax reform should cover capital gains - CDU.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) said on Tuesday Germany should tighten rules on capital gains taxes as part of a sweeping tax reform due to take effect in January 1999.
The CDU plan would cut taxes by a net 30 billion marks a year by lowering income tax rates, but it also aims to broaden the tax base and eliminate loopholes.
The CDU published its proposal as part of a process that will culminate at year-end in a plan by a tax reform commission headed by Finance Minister Theo Waigel.

The CDU plan would slash Germany's top income tax rate to 35 percent from the current 53 percent, and lower taxes by up to 30 billion marks in 1999, Wolfgang Schaeuble, head of the CDU/CSU parliamentary faction, told a news conference.

"Our goal, which is shared by Finance Minister Waigel and the Free Democratic Party, is a net tax reduction and a broadening of the tax base," Schaeuble said. Reform would strengthen Germany's international competitiveness and boost jobs, the CDU said in a position paper.
Schaeuble said the CDU plan is broadly in line with an outline put forward on Monday by Waigel, who said he saw the top rate falling to 35 to 40 percent.
The CDU plan would tax capital gains on all sales of securities or real estate, not just "speculative" sales of assets held less than six months, the current German practice.
"That is an unequal treatment of income. The point is to treat it the same," Schaeuble said. An exception would be made for primary residences.
The CDU plan would restrict companies' leeway to set aside tax-free reserves, and limit depreciation write-offs.
The plan also calls for the elimination of current tax exemptions for income from Sunday, holiday or night work. Rules on business expenses would be tightened.
Church tax and charitable donations would continue to be deductible.
The CDU plan would cut the minimum income tax rate to less than 20 percent from the current 26 percent.
The CDU will present the plan at a party congress at the end of the month.
